memo: We recommend closing Plant 6 and relocating the product family to the remaining plants. This option delivers the greatest incremental operating income (+$16.5 million per year) and requires only a one‑time $10 million capital outlay to move equipment. The plant’s current loss of $9 million after corporate allocations will be eliminated, and the corporate cost allocation of $32.4 million remains with the Company, further improving margins. To preserve talent and limit severance costs, we will move the maximum 29 employees the other plants can absorb. Relocation assistance of $20,000 per employee will cost $560,000. The remaining 161 employees will receive the standard severance of $4,566 each, totaling about $735,000. Combined, the workforce transition cost is roughly $1.3 million—small compared with the $16.5 million annual operating‑income boost. The product family’s revenue is retained, and the other plants have capacity for the added $361 million of revenue. This strategy maximizes shareholder value over the next four quarters while staying well within the Company’s $444.9 million liquidity cushion.

We have selected the "close" option for Plant 6. Closing the plant eliminates its negative operating result and, by moving the product family to the remaining facilities, lifts Company operating income by $16.5 million annually – the largest earnings boost of the three alternatives. The cash impact is modest: a one‑time $10 million relocation cost plus $580 k for moving 29 employees and $735 k in severance for the 161 eliminated staff, leaving a net cash inflow of roughly $5.2 million after the first year. This improves both earnings and cash generation, supporting the board’s objective of creating shareholder value over the next four quarters. The relocation capacity is limited to 29 employees, which we fully utilise; the remaining 161 positions are eliminated with the standard severance package. The decision preserves the product family’s revenue, avoids the $15.3 million earnings drag of a sale, and requires no large capital outlay like the $30 million retooling. In sum, closing Plant 6 maximises operating profit while delivering a positive cash contribution and minimal disruption to the broader workforce.

We selected the "sell" option for Plant 6 because it delivers the greatest short‑term shareholder value over the next four quarters. The sale provides an immediate cash inflow of $37.5 million and, after accounting for the one‑time relocation assistance ($3.42 million) and severance for the 19 eliminated workers ($0.09 million), the net cash impact is roughly +$18.7 million. Although the plant’s loss will reduce operating income by $15.3 million annually, this reduction is already reflected in the net cash calculation and is outweighed by the cash proceeds and lower payroll. 

We will transfer the maximum 171 employees to the buyer, the only line available under the sell scenario, and offer relocation assistance of $20,000 per person. The remaining 19 employees will be eliminated with the standard severance package of $4,566 each. This allocation respects all line limits and fully utilizes the buyer’s capacity while keeping the total headcount at 190.

The decision preserves liquidity, improves free cash flow for the year, and aligns with the board’s objective of creating shareholder value in the near term.

We recommend closing Plant 6 and relocating the product family to the remaining plants.  Closing generates a $16.5 million annual boost to operating income and eliminates the plant’s $10.5 million payroll, while the $10 million one‑time closure cost is modest.  The net effect in the first year is a cash inflow of roughly $5.2 million after accounting for severance ($161 × $4,566 ≈ $0.74 M) and relocation ($29 × $20,000 ≈ $0.58 M).  Over the next four quarters the operating‑income uplift outweighs these one‑off costs, creating clear shareholder value.  The other plants have capacity for the additional revenue, but can only absorb 29 of Plant 6’s workers; the remaining 161 employees will receive severance.  This allocation respects the maximums (29 moved, 161 eliminated) and uses the available liquidity well within the $444.9 million cushion.  By closing the loss‑making site we remove the $32.9 million excess cost, improve margins, and preserve cash for strategic investments, aligning with the board’s objective of maximizing shareholder returns in the short term.

We have selected the "close" option for Plant 6. Closing the plant eliminates its $9.0 M operating loss and, by shifting production to the higher‑margin plants, lifts Company operating income by $16.5 M annually – the greatest upside of the three alternatives. The one‑time closure cost of $10 M is modest relative to the $44.1 M cash cushion and the $300 M undrawn credit facility, leaving ample liquidity. To retain talent, we will relocate the maximum 29 employees to other plants (cost $580 k in relocation assistance). The remaining 161 positions will be eliminated, incurring severance of $4,566 per employee ($≈$735 k). These one‑off workforce costs total under $2 M, far outweighed by the $16.5 M per‑year boost to operating income and the removal of the $10.5 M payroll burden. The closure also eliminates the plant’s $9.4 M payroll and avoids future fixed‑cost overruns. Over the next four quarters, the net effect is a substantial increase in earnings, higher free cash flow, and stronger returns for shareholders, fully aligning with the board’s objective to create shareholder value.

We have elected to sell Plant 6 and its product family. The sale generates a one‑time cash inflow of $37.5 million, which can be redeployed to accelerate share repurchases or dividend growth, directly enhancing shareholder value in the next four quarters. Although the transaction reduces operating income by $15.3 million annually (after‑tax impact of roughly $12 million), the net cash benefit after accounting for the $0.09 million severance cost on the 19 eliminated employees is still about $25 million, a material boost to liquidity. The buyer will retain 171 of the 190 positions for at least two years, preserving the majority of the workforce and minimizing disruption. The remaining 19 employees will receive severance of $4,566 each, a modest cost relative to the cash proceeds. This approach balances the need to improve the balance sheet and return capital to shareholders while limiting job losses. The alternative options—retooling or closing—either require large capital outlays with modest operating gains or result in a smaller cash benefit and higher ongoing costs. Selling therefore maximizes immediate shareholder return while managing the workforce impact responsibly.

Employee impact is handled within the limits set by the board. Of the 190 workers, we will relocate the maximum 29 employees to other plants, paying $20,000 relocation assistance each ($580,000 total). The remaining 161 positions will be eliminated with the standard severance of $4,566 per employee ($735,126 total). These one‑time outlays (~$1.3 million) are outweighed by the annual operating income gain and the $10 million closure expense, creating net value for shareholders over the next four quarters.

The decision also preserves the product family’s revenue stream, leverages existing capacity at the other plants, and aligns with the board’s objective of maximizing shareholder returns.
